title: Although: aunque and facts that contrast

sections.title: What you already know
sections.content: You know *aunque* ("although") from A2 Unit 28. It joins two facts that seem to pull in different directions. When both are facts of the past, the verb after *aunque* is in the indicative: *Aunque la red de trenes crecía, los precios se decidían en Europa.*

items.spanish: Aunque los ferrocarriles unían los puertos con el interior, muchas líneas no unían unas regiones con otras.
items.english: Although the railways joined the ports with the interior, many lines did not join one region with another.

items.spanish: Aunque la red de trenes crecía, los precios de los productos se decidían en los mercados de Europa.
items.english: Although the railway network was growing, the prices of the products were decided in the markets of Europe.

items.spanish: Aunque el enclave daba trabajo a mucha gente, una parte de las ganancias salía del país.
items.english: Although the enclave gave work to many people, part of the profits left the country.

items.spanish: Muchas líneas no unían las regiones, aunque los ferrocarriles unían los puertos con el interior.
items.english: Many lines did not join the regions, although the railways joined the ports with the interior.

sections.content: The *aunque* clause can come first or second. When it comes first, put a comma after it. The main idea is the clause that is *not* introduced by *aunque*.
